issues.legal_issue: A consumer forum may hear an eligible consumer’s complaint about a real-estate project even when a remedy is available under real-estate regulation law.
material_facts: The apartment purchasers brought complaints before the consumer commission, seeking refunds because the project had not been completed on time.
The project was registered under the real-estate regulatory law after the purchasers had entered into their agreements.
The developer argued that the regulatory authorities had exclusive jurisdiction and that the consumer commission could not entertain the complaints.
issues.conclusion: The regulatory law did not bar the consumer commission from entertaining the complaints; the remedies available under consumer law remained available alongside the regulatory remedy.
issues.legal_principle: Consumer Protection Act, 1986, Sections 3 and 12(4), preserve additional consumer remedies and prevent transfer of an admitted complaint to another forum. Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, Sections 18, 71, 79, 88 and 89 do not displace those remedies: Section 79 bars civil courts, not consumer fora, and Sections 18 and 88 preserve other remedies. The Court relied on Secretary, Thirumurugan Cooperative Agricultural Credit Society v. M. Lalitha; National Seeds Corporation Ltd. v. M. Madhusudhan Reddy; Virender Jain v. Alaknanda Cooperative Group Housing Society Ltd.; Emaar MGF Ltd. v. Aftab Singh; Malay Kumar Ganguli v. Dr. Sukumar Mukherjee; and Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India.

predicates.consumer_complaint: An allottee files a complaint in a consumer forum about a service connected with a real-estate purchase.
predicates.eligible_consumer: The complainant qualifies as a consumer in relation to the transaction.
predicates.real_estate_regulatory_remedy_available: A regulatory law provides the allottee with a remedy concerning the same real-estate dispute.
predicates.consumer_forum_jurisdiction_not_barred: The consumer forum is not barred from hearing the complaint merely because the regulatory remedy is available.

issues.definition: When an eligible consumer brings a consumer complaint about a real-estate dispute for which a regulatory remedy is also available, the consumer forum may still hear the complaint.

issues.legal_issue: Registration of a delayed real-estate project does not postpone an allottee’s entitlement to pursue a claim based on the completion date in the agreement.
material_facts: The purchasers entered into their agreements before the project was registered under the real-estate regulatory law.
The contractual period for completing construction had expired before registration.
The developer relied on the later registration’s validity period to argue that it had not yet delayed construction.
issues.conclusion: The later registration did not defer the purchasers’ entitlement; that entitlement had to be assessed under the terms of their agreements.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 18 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, under which the relevant completion date is the date specified in the agreement. It also relied on the registration certificate’s terms, which preserved an allottee’s right to return of the amount with interest if possession was not given in accordance with the agreement.

predicates.allottee_claim_based_on_agreement: An allottee bases a claim on the promised completion or possession terms in an agreement with the developer.
predicates.project_registered_after_contractual_dea: The project was registered under a regulatory scheme after the agreement’s completion deadline had passed.
predicates.registration_validity_period_extends_bey: The project’s regulatory registration remains valid beyond the deadline specified in the agreement.
predicates.registration_does_not_defer_allottee_ent: The later registration does not postpone the allottee’s entitlement to pursue a claim based on the agreement.

issues.definition: When an allottee relies on an agreement whose completion deadline passed before the project’s later registration, a registration period extending beyond that deadline does not defer the allottee’s entitlement.

issues.legal_issue: Consumer proceedings and compatible actions taken under the repealed consumer law remain effective under the successor consumer law.
material_facts: The purchasers initiated consumer proceedings under the 1986 consumer law.
The consumer commission issued orders in those proceedings.
The successor consumer law had come into force, and the developer challenged whether the earlier proceedings and orders remained effective.
issues.conclusion: The proceedings and resulting actions, including the consumer commission’s orders, were saved.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 100 and 107 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 preserve the additional character of consumer remedies and save actions taken under the repealed Consumer Protection Act, 1986 to the extent they are not inconsistent with the successor law. The Court also referred to Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.

predicates.consumer_proceeding_under_repealed_law: A consumer complaint was initiated under a consumer law that was later repealed.
predicates.action_taken_in_that_proceeding: A consumer forum took an action or issued an order in the proceeding before or in connection with the repeal.
predicates.action_not_inconsistent_with_successor_l: The earlier action or order is not inconsistent with the successor consumer law.
predicates.proceeding_and_action_remain_saved: The proceeding and compatible actions taken in it remain effective under the successor law.

issues.definition: A proceeding initiated under a repealed consumer law, and compatible actions taken in it, remain effective under the successor law.

issues.legal_issue: Purchasers who acquire apartments for personal residential use, rather than commercial profit, qualify as consumers.
material_facts: The purchasers said that each had acquired one residential apartment for personal use and that most had taken home loans.
The developer contended that the apartments had been acquired for investment or profit.
The consumer commission found the purchasers to be consumers, and the Supreme Court upheld that finding.
issues.conclusion: The consumer commission correctly found the complainants to be consumers.
issues.legal_principle: The Court upheld the finding under the definition of “consumer” in Section 2(d) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. It noted the purchasers’ evidence of personal residential use and found no basis to disturb the commission’s conclusion.

predicates.appeal_against_consumer_forum_order: A party appeals from an order of a consumer forum concerning an apartment purchase.
predicates.apartment_acquired_for_personal_residenc: The purchaser acquired the apartment for personal residential use.
predicates.no_commercial_profit_purpose: The apartment was not acquired for a commercial or profit-making purpose.
predicates.purchaser_qualifies_as_consumer: The purchaser qualifies as a consumer in relation to the apartment transaction.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a consumer-forum order, a purchaser who acquired an apartment for personal residence and not commercial profit qualifies as a consumer.

issues.legal_issue: A developer’s failure to deliver possession by the agreed deadline, without substantiated events excusing the delay, supports a finding of deficient service.
material_facts: The agreed period for completing construction had expired, but the project remained incomplete.
The developer acknowledged delay and relied on matters including labour shortages, delays in obtaining approvals, and demonetisation to explain it.
The consumer commission found that the developer had not provided evidence establishing force majeure events, and the Supreme Court upheld the findings of delay and deficiency.
issues.conclusion: The consumer commission’s findings that the developer delayed completion and was deficient in service were correct and did not warrant interference.
issues.legal_principle: The Court upheld the consumer commission’s determination of deficiency in service in light of the expired contractual completion period, the admitted delay, the absence of proof substantiating force majeure, and the agreement’s provisions concerning delay and failure to deliver possession, including Clauses 11.4 and 41.

rule.if: appeal_against_consumer_order and contractual_completion_deadline_expired and possession_not_delivered and developer_failed_to_substantiate_excusing_events

predicates.appeal_against_consumer_order: A developer appeals from a consumer-forum order concerning delayed possession of an apartment.
predicates.contractual_completion_deadline_expired: The completion or possession deadline specified in the agreement has passed.
predicates.possession_not_delivered: The developer has not delivered possession of the apartment by the agreed deadline.
predicates.developer_failed_to_substantiate_excusin: The developer relied on events to excuse the delay but did not substantiate that those events caused or excused the failure to deliver on time.
predicates.delay_and_deficiency_finding_upheld: The finding that the developer delayed delivery and provided deficient service is upheld.

issues.definition: When the contractual deadline has passed, possession remains undelivered, and the developer has not substantiated events excusing the delay, the finding of delay and deficient service is upheld.
